issues.display_title: Issue #276: Investigation of Post-Authentication OAuth URL Parameters on a Local Callback Server
issues.main_description_html:
Result from Developer

Yes, that is correct and expected behavior.

Why localhost:<port> is used:

For desktop applications, Google OAuth follows the RFC 8252 (OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps) standard via a local loopback callback (http://localhost:<port>):

  1. When starting the Google sign-in process, the desktop app spins up a temporary HTTP listener on an ephemeral port on 127.0.0.1.
  2. The user signs in via their default system browser.
  3. Google redirects back to http://localhost:<port>/?code=..., allowing the application's backend to capture the authorization code, immediately close the listener, and exchange the code for session tokens securely.
  4. This is the official industry best practice used by desktop clients like VS Code, GitHub CLI, and Slack.

Note on the previous flow:

Previously, the app used an intermediate web redirect via https://app.gothru.co/auth-gothru-photo-studio, which forwarded the authorization code via a custom deep link (gothru-photo-studio://auth-google?token=...). However, that approach had notable limitations:

  • Human error & popup blockers: If a user accidentally clicked "Cancel" on the browser's "Open GoThru Photo Studio?" confirmation prompt or if their browser blocked pop-ups, the desktop app would hang indefinitely waiting for the authentication response.
  • Cancellation handling: If the user canceled the login on Google's screen, the web forwarder never triggered the deep link back to the app.

The current local loopback flow avoids intermediate browser prompts and deep-link handoff issues, providing the highest reliability, stability, and seamless UX.
